# Step 1: Ensure instrument sensitivity

## Importing experimental data

```{r import}
calibration <- read.csv("Ethyl Carbamate/EC_calibration.csv")
```

## Assessing model fit by plotting residuals

Evaluate how the model residuals confirm/deny what we observed visually

```{r residuals, echo=FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%", warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Example using HPLC method
# We first want to fit our data with a linear model using the function lm()

fit_HPLC <- lm(fluor_signal_area ~ conc_ug_L, calibration)

#then we plot the output of the residuals calculated by that model
ggplot(fit_HPLC, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Fitted - HPLC", x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16)


#now do the same for the GC method!


```

## Grubbs test

Can we remove any outliers in our calibration data?

```{r Grubbs, echo = FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%"}

#For the HPLC calibration curve, we want to look at the lowest value when the concentration is 10 ug/L
Grubbs_HPLC <- calibration %>%
  filter(conc_ug_L == 10) %>%
  summarize(mean_HPLC = mean(fluor_signal_area), 
            sd_HPLC = sd(fluor_signal_area))

G_HPLC <- abs(220.5- Grubbs_HPLC$mean_HPLC)/Grubbs_HPLC$sd_HPLC

print(paste("The calculated G value of", round(G_HPLC, 3), "is higher than the critical value of 1.672, and thus the data point can be removed", sep = " "))

calibration[which(calibration$fluor_signal_area == 220.5), 'fluor_signal_area'] <- NA

#For the GC data, we want to look at the high value when the concentration is 10 ug/L
#do it here!






#Let's re-check our residuals plot!

# Example using HPLC method
# We first want to fit our data with a linear model using the function lm()

fit_HPLC <- lm(fluor_signal_area ~ conc_ug_L, calibration)

#then we plot the output of the residuals calculated by that model
ggplot(fit_HPLC, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Fitted - HPLC", x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16)


#now do the same for the GC method!



```

## Checking for linearity

One of our calibration curves does not look linear. How can we modify it to improve model performance?

```{r linearity, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%", echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message=FALSE}

#Let's try removing some of our high-concentration points that start deviating from the linear range
ggplot(calibration %>% filter(conc_ug_L < 40), aes(conc_ug_L, ms_signalintensity)) +
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
  theme_bw(base_size = 16)+
  ggtitle("Current GC calibration curve")

fit_GC <- lm(ms_signalintensity ~ `conc_ug_L`, calibration %>% filter(conc_ug_L < 40))
mod_sum_GC <- summary(fit_GC)
mod_sum_GC

#residuals plot
ggplot(fit_GC, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs Fitted", x = "Fitted Values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 16)

calibration[which(calibration$conc > 40), 'ms_signalintensity'] <- NA
```


## Calculating LOD and LOQ

```{r LOD, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
#Here is a table where we can store and sort all the data we calculate. 
limits <- tibble(
  type = c("LOD (method 1)", "LOD (method 2)", "LOQ (method 1)", "LOQ (method 2)"), 
  HPLC = as.double(1:4), 
  GC = as.double(1:4)
)

# Here is an example of the math for the HPLC method

#Calculating LOD and LOQ (method 1!)
limits[1, "HPLC"] <- round(3.3*mod_sum_HPLC$sigma/as.numeric(mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients["conc_ug_L", "Estimate"]), 3)

limits[3, "HPLC"] <- 10*mod_sum_HPLC$sigma/as.numeric(mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients["conc_ug_L", "Estimate"])

#Calculating LOD and LOQ (method 2!)
sd <- calibration %>%
  filter(conc_ug_L == 10) %>%
  select(fluor_signal_area) %>% 
  summarize(sd = sd(fluor_signal_area, na.rm = TRUE))

limits[2, "HPLC"] <- 3.3*as.numeric(sd)/as.numeric(mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients["conc_ug_L", "Estimate"])
limits[4, "HPLC"] <- 10*as.numeric(sd)/as.numeric(mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients["conc_ug_L", "Estimate"])

# Now, go do it for the GC method!




knitr::kable(limits, caption = "All calculated limits of detection", digits = 3,  format.args = list(drop0trailing = TRUE), format = "html", col.names = c(" ", "HPLC (\u00B5g/L)", "GC (\u00B5g/L)"))%>%
  column_spec(1:ncol(limits), extra_css = "padding-left: 30px; padding-right: 30px;")

```

# Step 2: Control experiments

## Standard Addition Experiments

We can use standard addition experiments to find systematic errors in our calibration curve. If you add 5 µL of a 1400 µg/mL solution to an initial volume of 1 mL of our wine sample four times, what is the initial concentration of ethyl carbamate?

```{r SA, echo = FALSE, fig.show="hold", out.width="50%", warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#First, we have to plot our standard addition curve to obtain our linear plot. 
SA <- calibration %>%
  select(SA_HPLC, spike_uL) %>%
  mutate(spike_mL = spike_uL/1000,
         x = 1250*(spike_mL/1), 
         y = SA_HPLC*(1 + spike_mL)/1)

#If we were doing this properly, we would evaluate model fit in the way we did before
ggplot(SA, aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")+
  theme_bw(base_size = 16) + 
  ylim(0,600)

fit <- lm(y ~ x, SA)
mod_sum_SA <- summary(fit)
mod_sum_SA

SA_conc = mod_sum_SA$coefficients[1,1]/mod_sum_SA$coefficients[2,1]
calc_conc = as.numeric((calibration[1,"SA_HPLC"]- mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[1,1])/mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[1,2])

#this is handwavy, but we will discuss more rigorous comparisons later. Ultimately, you want to do a t-test.
print(paste("The concentration determined by the standard addition is", round(SA_conc, 2), "\u00B5g/L which is similar to the concentration calculated with the calibration curve of", round(calc_conc, 2), "\u00B5g/L", sep = " "))
```

## Spike and recovery experiments

We want to make sure our sample preparation does not gain or lose ethyl carbamate. We add the equivalent of 90 µg/mL into our wine. What is our recovery %, based on the recovery data we collected?

```{r SR, echo = FALSE}

# Let's assume we are using the same wine sample as the one we used for our standard addition. One has additional ethyl carbamate that we added (recovery), and other one doesn't (spike = 0)

#Let's calculate the final concentration of ethyl carbamate for both samples using our calibration curve
SR <- calibration %>%
  filter(spike_uL == 0) %>%
  select(SA_HPLC, recovery_HPLC) %>%
    mutate(SA_HPLC = (SA_HPLC - mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[1,1])/mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[2,1], 
         recovery_HPLC = (recovery_HPLC - mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[1,1])/mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[2,1], 
         SA_HPLC = SA_HPLC*1.3*3,
         recovery_HPLC = recovery_HPLC*1.3*3) %>%
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))

recovery = (SR$recovery_HPLC - SR$SA_HPLC)/90*100

#Again, we are not reporting our uncertainty because we will cover it soon
print(paste("Our recovery is ", round(recovery, 2), "%"))
```

# Step 3: Identifying and reporting uncertainty

## HPLC method

### Unknown Concentrations

It's finally time to 'officially' calculate the concentration of ethyl carbamate in two wine samples, WineA and WineB.

```{r HPLC_unknown, echo = FALSE}
unknown_HPLC <- calibration %>%
  mutate(HPLC_concA = (unknownA_HPLC - mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[1,1])/mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[2,1], 
         HPLC_concB = (unknownB_HPLC - mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[1,1])/mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[2,1]) 

unknownA_HPLC <- mean(unknown_HPLC$HPLC_concA, na.rm = TRUE)
unknownA_HPLC_wine <- unknownA_HPLC*3.3*1.3

print(paste("The concentration of ethyl carbamide in wine A is ", round(unknownA_HPLC, 3), " ug/L which corresponds to a concentration in the wine of", round(unknownA_HPLC_wine, 3), " ug/L"))

#Now, do the calculation on your own!





```

### Calculating the standard deviation of the measurement

```{r HPLC uncertainty, echo = FALSE}
sy = mod_sum_HPLC$sigma
m = mod_sum_HPLC$coefficients[2,1]
k = 5
n = 11
y = unknownA_HPLC
y_cal = as.numeric(unknown_HPLC %>%
                   filter(conc_ug_L > 7)  %>%
                   summarize(mean = mean(conc_ug_L, na.rm = TRUE)))
us = as.numeric(unknown_HPLC %>%
                   filter(conc_ug_L > 7)  %>%
                   summarize(sd = sd(conc_ug_L, na.rm = TRUE)))


muA_HPLC = sy/m*sqrt((1/k) +
          (1/7) +
           (unknownA_HPLC - y_cal)^2/(m^2*us^2*(n-1)))

#This doesn't account for the dilution! We have to propagate our uncertainty from our calibration to the final concentration by accounting for dilution. 

muA_HPLC_wine <- muA_HPLC/unknownA_HPLC*unknownA_HPLC_wine

print(paste("The ethyl carbamate concentration in our sample is ", round(unknownA_HPLC, 1) , " \u00B1 ", round(muA_HPLC, 1), " \u00B5g/L from n = ", k, ", and a concentration in Wine A of", round(unknownA_HPLC_wine, 1), " \u00B1 ", round(muA_HPLC_wine, 1), " \u00B5g/L from n = ", k, sep = " "))

#now do it yourself for wine B!





```

### Calculating the 95% confidence interval

```{r CI HPLC, echo = FALSE}

CI_HPLC_wineA <- muA_HPLC_wine*3.182

print(paste("The ethyl carbamate concentration in Wine A is ", round(unknownA_HPLC_wine, 1) , " \u00B5g/L, 95% CI [", round(unknownA_HPLC_wine-CI_HPLC_wineA, 1), ",", round(unknownA_HPLC_wine+CI_HPLC_wineA, 1), "]" , sep = ""))

# your turn for WineB


```

# Step 4: evaluating results

Do the measurements with the GC and the HPLC give us the same result? Are Wine A and Wine B the same?

## F-test:

This tells us if the standard deviations statistically different

### Comparing two methods

```{r, echo = FALSE}
#Let's calculate the F value for Wine A

F_wineA = muA_HPLC_wine^2/muA_GC_wine^2
print(paste("The calculated F value of", round(F_wineA, 2), "is lower that the F table value of 6.39, so the standard deviations are not significantly different", sep = " "))

#Now do it for wine B!


```

### Comparing two wines

```{r, echo = FALSE}
F_HPLC = muB_HPLC_wine^2/muA_HPLC_wine^2
print(paste("The calculated F value of", round(F_HPLC, 2), "is lower that the F table value of 6.39, so the standard deviations are not significantly different", sep = " "))

#you do it for the GC

```

## t-test:

This tells us if the means of the two categories are statistically different. We use different equations to calculate the t-value, depending on if the standard deviations are significantly different or not. Here, because they are not different, we can use the standard Student's t-test equation.

### Comparing two methods

```{r t test method, echo = FALSE}
t_wineA = abs(unknownA_HPLC_wine - unknownA_GC_wine)*sqrt(5*5/(5+5))/sqrt((muA_HPLC_wine^2*4+ muA_GC_wine^2*4)/(8))
print(paste("The calculated t value of", round(t_wineA, 2), "is higher that the t-table value of 2.306, so the means are significantly different", sep = " "))

#Now, you do it for WineB!


```

### Comparing two wines

```{r sample comparison, echo = FALSE}
t_HPLC = abs(unknownA_HPLC_wine - unknownB_HPLC_wine)*sqrt(5*5/(5+5))/sqrt((muA_HPLC_wine^2*4+ muB_HPLC_wine^2*4)/(8))
print(paste("The calculated t value of", round(t_HPLC, 2), "is higher that the t-table value of 2.306, so the means are significantly different", sep = " "))

#you do it for the GC


```

## Built in R functions

Why isn't there an easier way to do this? Without taking into account the uncertainty of our measurement, the data suggests we are less uncertain than we actually are!

```{r R functions for stats, echo = FALSE}

#This is what we calculate
print(paste("The F-test value comparing wine A and B as measured by the GC is", round(F_GC, 3), "and the t-test result is", round(t_GC, 3), "which indicates the means are statistically different, but the standard deviations are not.", sep = " "))

#this is how we have to do it in R - using our replicates as independent values
var.test(calibration$unknownA_GC,calibration$unknownB_GC)
t.test(calibration$unknownA_GC,calibration$unknownB_GC, var.equal = TRUE)
```

When I individually convert all my signals into concentrations with my calibration curve data, and *then* find the standard deviation, I find my standard deviation is `round(as.numeric(unknown_GC %>%   mutate(GC_concA = GC_concA*10/2) %>%   summarize(sd = sd(GC_concA, na.rm = TRUE))), 3)`. When I propagate my replicates through the uncertainty of my calibration curve, I find a standard deviation of `round(muA_GC, 3)`.
